title: There or not there? A multidisciplinary review and research agenda on the impact of transparent barriers on human perception, action, and social behavior

findings.quote: humans are surprisingly skilled at seeing transparent structures even in the absence of such opaque markers. However, the visual perception of transparent barriers seems largely guided by perceivers' experience-based expectations of where to find them

findings.antecedent: Specific luminance differences between neighboring parts of a surface
findings.consequent: Perception of transparency (one surface seen through another)
findings.quote: Metelli demonstrated that specific luminance differences between neighboring parts of a surface would induce the impression that some parts were seen directly, whereas others were seen through a transparent layer
contours aligned in the way of an X-junction [...] indicate transparency

findings.antecedent: Transparent barriers (clear, smooth, faultless, frameless panes)
findings.quote: Unsurprisingly, undetected transparent barriers can pose a serious health and safety risk. Accidents due to collisions with glass doors or walls have been reported for both children and adults

findings.antecedent: Conflicting tactile (impenetrable) and visual (permeable) information from transparent barriers within peripersonal space
findings.quote: Initial evidence indicates that when faced with conflicting information coming from tactile and visual sensors, humans rely more strongly on the latter, especially when the sensory contradictions arise within a person's peripersonal space

findings.antecedent: Transparent barriers between perceiver and approaching objects/people
findings.consequent: Suppression of physical arousal and motor reflexes (e.g., defensive withdrawal, tactile extinction)
findings.quote: the ineffectiveness of transparent barriers to interfere with basic reflexes is regularly taken advantage of in medical examinations.

The first study on distance estimation, for instance, revealed that preschoolers exaggerated distances between objects separated by both opaque as well as transparent barriers, whereas adults only exaggerated distances across opaque barriers (Kosslyn et al., 1974). A subsequent study demonstrated that neither adults, nor school-aged children overestimated distances between objects separated by transparent barriers (Herman et al., 1987).

findings.antecedent: Transparent barriers (vs. opaque barriers) obstructing a path (in infants)
findings.consequent: Detour ability / selection of alternative path
findings.quote: up to 10-months of age, infants displayed significant difficulty in detour ability when obstructed by a transparent barrier. Specifically, they hesitated or refused to select an alternative path to a goal when their current path was blocked ‘merely' by something transparent

findings.antecedent: Transparent barriers (vs. opaque barriers) for toy retrieval (in infants)
findings.quote: children younger than 10 months of age tried to directly reach for toys 'through' transparent surfaces, even though they readily reached around opaque barriers.

findings.antecedent: Transparent barriers (vs. opaque barriers) for barrier crossing (in toddlers)
findings.quote: Both 12- and 18-month-olds were found to successfully cross opaque barriers at larger thresholds than transparent barriers, suggesting that a child's ability to perform an adequate motor response suffers when faced with transparency

findings.antecedent: Transparent surface covering a 'visual cliff' (in infants)
findings.quote: infants capable of crawling typically hesitated to cross the surface, despite encouragement from a parent on the other side of the cliff.

findings.antecedent: Transparent barriers (vs. no barrier) separating strangers
findings.consequent: Comfort with close proximity / altered interpersonal distance preferences
findings.quote: By enabling the visual processing of others while preventing a physical interaction, transparent barriers may alter how we respond to the proximity of strangers

findings.antecedent: Transparent barriers (vs. no barrier) separating strangers
findings.consequent: Inclination to stare longer / comfort with being gazed at
findings.quote: Are people inclined to stare longer at others through transparent barriers, knowing that under these conditions they can gather social information without the obligation to engage in any further exchange? Equally important is the questions of whether targets of prolonged looks may be more comfortable with attracting someone's gaze through a transparent barrier than when no barrier is present.

findings.antecedent: Spaces largely defined by transparent barriers (vs. non-transparent barriers)
findings.quote: Their visual permeability, however, may reduce a person's sense of confinement (Stamps, 2010). As a result, the same density level may reduce feelings of crowding in spaces largely defined by transparent barriers than in spaces defined by non-transparent barriers.

findings.antecedent: Content of views through surrounding transparent barriers (e.g., nature vs. built environment)
findings.consequent: Readiness to aggress / willingness to withdraw during social threat
findings.quote: Thus, a person's readiness to aggress against social threats encountered indoors may get reduced or amplified, depending on whether transparent barriers afford stress-reducing or stress-inducing views (e.g., exposure to nature versus built environments)

findings.antecedent: Brighter rooms (potentially due to transparent barriers)
findings.consequent: Social inhibition (reducing anti-social behavior, increasing prosocial behavior)
findings.quote: Brighter rooms, for instance, seem to facilitate social inhibition (Hirsh et al., 2011), an effect that can reduce anti-social behavior (such as aggression or dishonesty, see Page and Moss, 1976; Prentice-Dunn and Rogers, 1980; Zhong et al., 2010) but also prosocial behavior (such as the willingness to collaborate, see Steidle et al., 2013).

findings.antecedent: Openness and transparency in workplace settings (potentially due to transparent barriers)
findings.consequent: Productivity and innovation (by enhancing knowledge/skill exchange)
findings.quote: initial observations suggest that openness and transparency in workplace settings can facilitate productivity and innovation by enhancing the exchange of knowledge and skills between individuals

findings.antecedent: Employee preferences for privacy and defensible territories
findings.consequent: Interference with architectural ideals of transparency
findings.quote: employees' preferences and demands for privacy and defensible territories may interfere with architectural ideals of transparency

findings.antecedent: View to a natural setting through a window (vs. brick wall) for surgical patients
findings.quote: The results showed faster, less painful recovery for surgical patients with a windowed view to a natural setting than for those with a view of a brick wall.
